body_markdown:
We recently visited[Westech Performance](https://westechperformance.com/) in Jurupa Valley, California, to witness friend and automotive media personality David Freiburger dyno-test his latest project motor. Finding the right cam has been a process, and for this round, Freiburger switched to a hydraulic roller cam. These are not cheap parts; did the move pay off?


First, some context. Freiburger purchased this Mopar 383 V-8 as a fresh rebuild with a plan of installing it in his 1970 Plymouth Duster. After taking it apart and checking things out, he decided it needed a camshaft with less duration to maintain safe piston-to-valve clearance. He found a suitable cam with 216/228 degrees of duration at .050” valve lift, .454/.480 inches of total lift, and 112 degrees of lobe separation.


Earlier this week, we covered a bit of[the process that David went through to get his engine ready to run](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/watch-david-freiburger-fix-everything-wrong-with-his-cropduster-383/%E2%86%97) . At that time, the engine produced a respectable 445.5 lb-ft of torque at 3500 rpm and 396.1 hp at 5400 rpm, but the 440 Source aluminum cylinder heads held more potential. With the engine’s flat-top pistons taking a whole lot of longer-duration camshafts off the menu, Freiburger decided to install a roller camshaft and see if the 383 could be a little more impressive.


Comp Cams


Because of the mechanical interaction of a flat tappet cam lobe on a flat-tappet lifter, the lobe can’t be too aggressive. With a roller following the cam lobe rather than the nearly flat face of a stock lifter, a roller cam can both lift and lower the valve faster. So, for a given duration, the roller cam can offer more lift. Alternatively, it can offer equal lift with less duration, allowing for less overlap—the time in which both the intake and exhaust valves are open—even with an identical lobe separation angle.


The specs for this particular Summit Racing roller cam are 224/236 duration, .550/.550 lift, and a 110-degree lobe separation angle. That’s eight more degrees of duration on both the exhaust and intake, a bit more lift, plus the benefit of faster opening and closing rates on the valves. It’s not a direct A:B comparison, but you won’t find a roller cam with the exact duration specs the previous flat-tappet that Freiburger and Westech tested.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


After a few adjustments to the carb jets and a replacement for some sticky seats on the float bowls, the new cam proved a success. With 425 hp at 5800 rpm and 446 lb.-ft. of torque registering at 3400 rpm right when the dyno started recording, it produced more power pretty much everywhere the dyno charted. The small dip just after the beginning of the roller cam run can likely be attributed to the dyno servo catching up to the engine starting its run, but there’s evidence of solid gains across the board.


Peak torque is similar, although the new horsepower peak, at around 5800 rpm, shows that the new springs do a better job keeping the valves under control. The previous cam had power fall way off after 5500 rpm, likely due to valve float. This iteration of the engine could happily shift at 6000 rpm. It’s worth noting that pushing the power peak up by swapping to a cam with more duration often results in a loss of low-end power. This engine simply wanted a bigger cam. There just weren’t any downsides.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The four-circuit metering blocks of the Edelbrock VRS-4150 carburetor (right) can help tame a big cam. The mild 383 made just as much power running the budget-friendly Brawler 4150 mechanical-secondary carb.


Was it worth it? Let’s dig into the cost. If you’re debating the switch to a roller cam, the biggest expense will likely be the roller lifters, which require link bars to prevent them from rotating in their bores and causing damage to the cam lobe. The retrofit hydraulic roller lifters for this Mopar RB V-8 are currently in the $725-$800 range, with a camshaft running between $400 and $600. Compare that to $100-$200 for the hydraulic flat-tappet lifters and $200-$300 for the flat-tappet cam. Then there are new pushrods, a distributor gear that’s compatible with the camshaft, and new valve springs. Add things up, and the cost can be $2000 or more. That’s a lot to pay for a 30 horsepower gain in this case, especially since some of that gain can be attributed to the added duration.


The total price for your build will, of course, vary depending on the engine family in question. (Now, if your engine came from the factory with a roller cam, then the price of upgrading will be much less.) The other benefit of the roller cam, aside from its improved performance, is longevity. Maybe it is machining or metallurgy of modern cams and lifters, but many engine builders are wary of flat-tappet cams. We can certainly understand anyone who wants to invest a bit extra in their engine for the peace of mind a roller cam brings.


However, many enthusiasts are building a fun street engine and don’t care about every last horsepower, or squeezing every little bit of torque to knock the last tenth off their elapsed times. In that case, the spring pressure on the cam and lifters will be much lower. With the right break-in lubrication and zinc (ZDDP) performance oil, a flat-tappet cam might be the right choice.


**Engine:** Mopar 383 RB V-8


**Factory bore and stroke, in inches:** 4.25×3.375


**Final bore and stroke, in inches:** 4.31×3.375


**Displacement:** 393.9 cubic inches


**Compression Ratio:** 9.45:1


**Cylinder head:** 440 Source Stealth aluminum heads


**Camshaft:** Summit Racing SUM-5782


**Intake manifold:** Edelbrock Performer RPM


**Induction:** Brawler 4150 750CFM carburetor


**Peak power:** 425hp at 5800 rpm


**Peak torque:** 445 lb.-ft. at 3400 rpm
